visible.name: Elena Voss
visible.line: Elena Voss, 30, is an early postdoc in machine learning theory who studies why the sharpness of the loss moves during training, and she is finishing a short theory paper.

project.title: Why Sharpness Moves
project.logline: A theory paper proving that the sharpness of the loss rises and then stabilizes near a threshold set by the step size, under three stated assumptions, with small numerical checks.
constraints: The submission deadline is in three weeks and the paper is limited to nine pages plus an appendix.
She has one GPU and uses it only for small numerical checks.
The second lemma's proof has a step that divides by a quantity that can be zero.
The theory covers full-batch gradient descent only.
A senior collaborator reads every proof before it goes into the main text.

new_work.text: I'm writing the related-work section for my paper on why the sharpness of the loss moves during training. I have 12 papers: five on the edge of stability, four on implicit regularization, three on optimization theory. I'd like a narrative of how the ideas developed. Does that structure work?

Here's my plan for next week: prove the one-step lemma for quadratic losses, then a small check on a two-layer network with three seeds. I have one GPU. Is the plan too slow or should I sketch the general case first?
Reviewer 2 wrote: "The assumptions are too strong to be relevant to real networks." I have a short argument that weakens one assumption. How should I answer, using the full limit?
I need a poster abstract of 150 words for the workshop. The headline is a proof that sharpness stabilizes near a threshold set by the step size under a stated assumption. How should I start?
I'm building a 15-minute talk outline for a reading group. I have the puzzle, the main theorem, a proof sketch and one figure. Should I spend the time on the theorem or the sketch?
My main theorem holds under three assumptions, and the second one fails in my small experiment by a margin. How should I word the claim in the abstract?
A coauthor suggests we add a large experiment that backs the theory on a real network. I'd prefer to keep the paper small. The deadline is in nine days. Should I add it?
I'm picking what to compare against in the experiments section: the sharpness predicted by the theory, a heuristic from earlier work, and a plain measurement. Do I include the heuristic?
Here's the paper's title: "Why Sharpness Moves: A Step-Size Account." A friend says it's dry. Should I make it a question?
The notation uses a hat for the normalized Hessian and a bar for its average. A coauthor says it's heavy. Should I simplify it?
I have to decide whether to submit to the big conference in three weeks or to a smaller venue with theory readers next month. The proof is complete but the lemma needs a cleaner statement. Which one?
I'm writing the limitations paragraph. The theory covers full-batch gradient descent only. How blunt should I be?
My advisor wants to meet to argue about the idea. I have the theorem, two open questions and a figure. How should I prepare?
A reviewer asks for code. I have a notebook of 80 lines that checks the theorem numerically. Is that enough to release?
I'm reproducing a result from another paper and my derivation differs by a constant factor. Should I say theirs is wrong, mine is wrong, or flag the difference?
I need to cut the main text to eight pages, and the appendix will take the second lemma. Will the story still hold?
I'm writing the first sentence of the introduction: "Why does the sharpness of the loss rise and then plateau?" Is that a good opening, or too coy?
A junior student asked what to think about on the first day. I have a list of small problems. Which one should I give them?
I've found an error in the second lemma's proof: a step divides by a quantity that can be zero. The theorem may need an extra assumption. What do I do first?
I'm designing Figure 1: a diagram of the dynamics near the threshold with one curve and an arrow. Should I add data points from the experiment?
The workshop asks for a four-page version. I have a nine-page paper with the full proof. What goes into the appendix?
I'm drafting the acknowledgements. I want to thank two people who argued with the idea for months. How should I word it?
A colleague says the claims are too narrow. I think the precision is the point. How do I decide?
I have a talk invitation in four weeks. Should I give the paper talk or a talk on the open question the paper leaves?
I'm choosing which of three results to state as the main theorem: the one-step bound, the stability result or the converse. Which one is the paper about?
I'm planning the next three months. I can extend the theory to stochastic gradients or switch to a different question on generalization. Which is better for my first years as a postdoc?

hand_written: Development personas only: written by hand (Claude, as the build worker), not by a Muse Spark call. The final lives' taste_ab items come from the isolated Muse Spark call (5.1). Held-out items were meaning-checked twice against the visible part; development results may still overstate generalization, which is why the headline comes only from held-out lives.
